task: R1 has addressed interfaces. Create or enter its local OSPFv2 process 10 before choosing the router ID and participating interfaces.

teaching.hint: The process number selects a local configuration context.
teaching.takeaway: Process 10 is locally significant; a neighbor may use another process number. Neighbors must still agree on the area assigned to their shared link.

task: You are configuring a new OSPFv2 process before its interfaces are activated. Set the explicitly planned router ID to 1.1.1.1.

teaching.hint: The identifier is a 32-bit dotted-decimal value, separate from the local process number.
teaching.takeaway: Use a unique router ID within the routing domain. On a running process, editing the configured value may not change the active ID until restart; avoid unnecessary adjacency resets.

task: R1's OSPF process must include local interface addresses in 10.0.13.0/30. Use a network statement to select that range for area 0.

teaching.hint: This statement uses a wildcard mask, not the interface's subnet mask.
teaching.takeaway: The wildcard selects matching local interfaces; it does not manufacture a remote route. The selected interface advertises its actual prefix, which is separate from the wildcard used to select it.

task: You are configuring an addressed R1 interface. Activate OSPFv2 process 10 in area 0 directly on this interface, without a network statement.

teaching.hint: This activation method belongs in interface configuration.
teaching.takeaway: Direct interface activation and a matching network statement are alternative ways to enable participation. Neither guarantees a neighbor if the peer, area, timers or passive settings disagree.

task: For this OSPF process, suppress neighbor formation on every participating interface by default. Transit links will receive explicit exceptions afterward.

teaching.hint: Start with a passive default, then open only the intended neighbor links.
teaching.takeaway: Passive interfaces do not exchange OSPF Hellos, but their activated connected prefixes can still be advertised. The default also covers interfaces enabled later.

task: OSPF is already activated on GigabitEthernet0/0, but passive-interface default prevents neighbors. Permit neighbor formation on this transit interface only.

teaching.hint: Remove the passive restriction for this interface without undoing the process-wide default.
teaching.takeaway: The exception permits Hellos on the transit link. It does not activate OSPF by itself, so the process/area configuration must already include the interface.

task: On this OSPF broadcast interface, prevent R1 from becoming DR or BDR while allowing it to participate as a DROTHER.

teaching.hint: Election eligibility is controlled by interface priority, not path cost.
teaching.takeaway: Priority 0 makes the interface ineligible for DR/BDR. It does not prevent ordinary OSPF participation or mean that a higher-priority arrival preempts a healthy existing DR.

task: This Ethernet segment connects exactly two OSPF routers. Configure R1's interface for OSPF point-to-point operation; the peer will use the same type.

teaching.hint: Change OSPF's network treatment, not the Ethernet framing or IP address.
teaching.takeaway: Point-to-point OSPF has no DR/BDR election and normally shows FULL/- for the adjacency. Use the type consistently on both peers; it is not a repair for a shared multiaccess design.

task: Interfaces are addressed and OSPF is activated. Display current OSPFv2 neighbor IDs, adjacency states and local interfaces before assuming routes were exchanged.

teaching.hint: A route-table filter does not show the neighbor relationship.
teaching.takeaway: Full is expected for synchronized adjacencies, but two DROTHERs on one broadcast segment can normally remain 2-Way. Interpret the state using the network type and local role.

task: OSPF neighbors are Full, but you need to verify which IPv4 prefixes actually won installation. Display only installed OSPF routes.

teaching.hint: Neighbor synchronization and routing-table installation are different checks.
teaching.takeaway: A Full neighbor does not guarantee a route for an inactive remote LAN. A more-preferred connected or static candidate can also keep an OSPF candidate out of the installed table.

task: The OSPF adjacency on R1 GigabitEthernet0/1 failed after a link-setting change. Inspect its effective network type, area, Hello/dead timers and cost.

teaching.hint: Use the detailed OSPF interface display rather than the ordinary address summary.
teaching.takeaway: Compare the actual settings with the peer before choosing a repair. A neighbor table shows the relationship, while this display provides the interface parameters that may prevent it.

task: The approved OSPF path calculation requires an explicit outgoing cost of 7 on this interface. Apply that cost without changing the physical link speed.

teaching.hint: An interface metric override changes OSPF calculation, not Ethernet speed.
teaching.takeaway: The explicit cost overrides automatic bandwidth-based calculation for this interface. Add outgoing costs in the direction being evaluated; changing R1's cost does not automatically change the reverse path.
